items: Temperature: a rise in temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules, which lets them overcome the attractive forces, so viscosity falls.
Intermolecular forces: the stronger the intermolecular forces, the greater the viscosity, because the molecules cannot move around each other freely and the resistance to flow increases.

blocks.alt: Top left: a liquid whose surface molecules have red arrows pulling inward while an inner molecule is pulled equally all round. Top middle: liquid layers of different lengths sliding in a channel. Top right: three closed vessels showing vapour building above a liquid until evaporation and condensation balance. Bottom: curves of vapour pressure against temperature for diethyl ether, ethanol, water and ethylene glycol crossing the 760 torr line at their boiling points, with notes.
blocks.caption: Surface tension, viscosity, the evaporation-condensation equilibrium and vapour pressure curves with normal boiling points (original diagram after Figures 5.8 and 5.9 and Tables 5.3 and 5.4).
blocks.long_description: Surface molecules are pulled inward only, so the surface tightens like a skin; viscosity is friction between sliding layers. In a closed vessel vapour builds until it condenses as fast as the liquid evaporates, and its pressure then is the vapour pressure. The curves rise with temperature, and each liquid boils where its curve reaches the external pressure: diethyl ether at 34.6, ethanol at 78.3 and water at 100 degrees C at 760 torr, ethylene glycol far higher. Stronger intermolecular forces give lower vapour pressure, higher boiling point, higher surface tension and higher viscosity.
